text:
Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

The development comes amid increasing scrutiny of digital platforms over content regulation and compliance. On the one hand, there is freedom of the press and of expression, which is a fundamental right of Indian citizens under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. On the other, there is the regulation of a foreign national’s entry into and departure from India, which falls entirely under immigration law and the discretionary power of the executive. The issuing of a visa does not create a permanent or irrevocable right of entry.  The right to reside and settle in India under Article 19 belongs only to Indian citizens. text:
Most interesting cultural takeaways from Mumbai, India

1. The culture on supporting women is so strong & unbelievably more left than we make it out in the west

The streets are literally plastered with ads saying #menwillbemen & every security check (entering malls or thru airport etc) has a separate women only line where the officer checks you inside a curtained box

2. They don't drink iced cold water

The water served at restaurants was always uncomfortably room temperature, even when I asked for it iced they would put a single ice cube in it. I also didn't see a single local get anything iced and if it was an iced drink they would ask them to remove the ice

3. Way more people speak English than I would have expected (unlike Buenos Aires... lol)

Mostly lower blue collar workers could only speak Hindi (some small street side vendors, security guards, janitors, etc). The guys that owned small storefronts could all speak perfectly & were incredible salesmen too

4. Legal drinking age is 25

I didn't drink at all the entire trip & idk how strongly this is enforced but that's 4 yrs more than any other country I've ever been to (Dubai & Indonesia are both 21), and we out here complaining about 21 in the US

5. Sidewalks & crosswalks don't exist

There's no coordinated mechanism for when to cross, it's just playing crossy road every day and u gotta send it. Reminds me of Indonesia, the drivers are all trained to stop within 2 ft of distance so it's fine

Overall was very reminiscent of Bangkok, super busy streets & even worse traffic, lots of cute cafes & beautiful luxurious malls

Statement : Meta told the Home Ministry it acted against 61,000 posts in the fortnight after Chalo Sansad. IFF calls for the record to be made public.

New Delhi, 13 November 2026

Meta has told the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the cybercrime arm of the Ministry of Home Affairs, that it acted on more than 61,000 Facebook and Instagram posts it classified as violent and inciteful between 25 July and 7 August 2026, @ThePrintIndia reported on 12 November. That is about three posts a minute for 14 days. The period begins on the day the Education Minister resigned and the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) ended its protest at Jantar Mantar, five days after police used tear gas and a lathi charge against its Chalo Sansad march.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the absence of any public account of this action. Meta disclosed the figure to the Home Ministry at a meeting on 21 August, and it became public only because the minutes were filed in the Supreme Court's suo motu proceedings on digital arrest scams.. In IFF's assessment, the minutes record direct pressure from the Ministry of Home Affairs on the content Meta carries.

As per the report in The Print a meeting was chaired by Rajesh Kumar, I4C's chief executive, and followed reviews by the Union Home Secretary, a parliamentary committee and a court-monitored committee on digital arrests. Its scope was wider than financial fraud. 

According to ThePrint, I4C sought an in-person briefing on "how the algorithm amplifies or suppresses specific content and viral accounts", an analysis of bot networks across prominent handles, and Meta's draft guidelines on deepfakes and re-uploaded content for review.
The minutes, as reported, do not state what the 61,000 posts concerned. It is not known which agency, if any, flagged them, or which law or company rule Meta applied. I4C itself did not accept aggregate figures when Meta cited 70 lakh pieces of content removed, it asked for examples with links. Users and the public are entitled to the same detail.

Complaints received by IFF show what was being restricted on Instagram as the period began. Here we are relying on our own inbound queries and requests for pro-bono help and legal assistance.

1) On 23 July, a story about the protests shared by a private account with 137 followers was made unavailable in India through what Instagram described as "an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements" under the IT Rules, 2021.

2) On 24 July, a reel by the journalist Ila Kazmi showing a Delhi Police facial recognition van scanning protesters at Jantar Mantar was withheld on a notice from "The Government of India / Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", which referred her to the Government of India for any questions. The Delhi High Court has directed the Home Ministry, the IT Ministry, the Delhi Police and Meta to produce the notice and will next hear the case on 17 November.

3) On 28 July, three days after the minister's resignation, Instagram withheld a video published on 15 June by the current-affairs page Unmutezone under the title "Why Modi Can't Ask Dharmendra Pradhan to Resign?". Its editor reported that a second video was blocked on 3 August.

Press reports describe similar restrictions. Newslaundry reported that an interview by the journalist Yaqut Ali with a former CJP spokesperson, posted on 26 July, was blocked in India within minutes, and that Facebook reels on the protests by the creator Jyoti Yadav, including an interview with AAP's Sanjay Singh, were restricted. It later reported restrictions on Instagram posts by Scroll and The Hindu about pellet-gun victims in Kashmir. None of this content is violent or inciteful, and Meta has not said whether it forms part of the figure.

The Home Ministry is involved at each stage from notices under Section 79(3)(b) reach platforms through the Sahyog portal, which I4C operates where close to 1.95 lakh blocking orders were issued to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July 2026, most of them through the portal, and Meta has integrated its systems with it so that flagged content can be restricted without human review. On 27 July the Delhi Police, which reports to the Home Ministry, was reported to have directed platforms to remove posts it considered offensive to the Prime Minister. Meta's transparency report lists violence and incitement among the categories that I4C refers to it. A ministry that operates this channel and also reviews Meta's enforcement figures and algorithm is supervising online speech.

We regret to state that the Supreme Court's own proceedings have provided an avenue for such censorship without sufficient checks and balances. In the suo motu digital arrest case, in which it directed intermediaries to place their proposals before I4C, and in the Just Rights for Children Alliance matters, in which it indicated that platforms may lose safe harbour, the Court has largely acted as a facilitator of executive action rather than as an adjudicator of its constitutional limits. The objectives of curbing fraud and protecting children are legitimate, but the supervision they have enabled now extends to lawful speech and results in censorship without legal authority.

These restrictions do not have a basis in law and often executive rulemaking is being used to circumvent the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression. Section 79(3)(b) sets a condition for a platform's immunity and in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court confined it to court orders and government notifications within Article 19(2). The power to block lies in Section 69A, which requires written reasons, committee review and, following Tanul Thakur (2022), a copy of the order and a hearing for the author. Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules requires each intimation to state reasons, the provision, the unlawful act and the URL, and to be reviewed monthly by a Secretary-rank officer. These requirements cannot be met through an automated integration with a three-hour deadline, whatever share of the 61,000 posts came through Sahyog.

Further, we state that while it may constitute a category of harmful speech, "Violent and inciteful" is not a ground for state mandated censorship under Article 19(2). Shreya Singhal protects discussion and advocacy and permits restriction only at the stage of incitement; a video asking why a minister has not resigned is discussion. Nor is there any clear statutory basis for I4C to perform the function of review a platform's content guidelines or to ask which accounts its algorithm promotes.

Our demands

1) The Ministry of Home Affairs must publish the minutes of its meetings with Meta in 2026 and state how many of the 61,000 posts were flagged by I4C, the Delhi Police or any other agency through Sahyog.

2) Meta must publish a breakdown of the 61,000 posts by the rule or law applied, the action taken and the requesting authority, and give each affected user the notice on which it acted. Further monthly breakdowns with qualitative disclosure is necesary.

3) I4C must withdraw its requests to review Meta's draft guidelines and to be briefed on its algorithm. Oversight of this kind requires a law made by Parliament and may only be performed by an independent regulatory body with a clear mandate and objective.

4) The Union Government must publish the monthly Secretary-level reviews under Rule 3(1)(d) for July and August 2026.

5) Meta must end the automatic execution of government and police flags in India and provide human review, a reasoned notice and an opportunity to respond before any restriction.

Users whose posts or accounts were restricted in India in July or August 2026 may write to legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots of each notice.

Andres Cabrera-Sanchez (April 4, 2026)
On April 4, Honduran national Andres Cabrera-Sanchez was arrested for allegedly possessing a loaded and unserialized handgun and possessing cocaine during an inspection of a restaurant in Brentwood, New York. Cristobal Felipe-Sarmiento (April 9, 2026)

He was sentenced to twelve years of post-prison supervision and was required to register as a sex offender. He was also convicted of driving under the influence in 2014.
(DHS, April 2026; Statesman Journal, December 2016)
Luis Alfonzo Marcano-Marcano (April 12, 2026)
On April 12, police responded to a medical center in Mint Hill, North Carolina, after a pregnant woman who suffered a gunshot wound to her stomach was admitted. The victim’s unborn child was pronounced dead shortly after. According to investigators, Venezuelan national Luis Alfonzo Marcano-Marcano dropped his wife off at the medical center and then sped away. He was later arrested in the lobby, and investigators pieced together details of the story. According to Marcano-Marcano, the incident occurred at their house following a birthday party. He and his girlfriend were standing on the porch arguing when he grabbed his pistol and shot the ground next to her feet. He then left the gun on the railing and left. His girlfriend picked up the gun and tried putting it into her pocket but accidentally pulled the trigger and shot herself in the stomach. Marcano-Marcano admitted that the reason why he left the hospital was to go home and throw the pistol into the woods. Once in custody, ICE lodged a detainer against him.
(ABC 7, April 2026; WCNC, April 2026; WXII 12, April 2026)
Eri Otoniel Roblero-Perez (April 12, 2026)
On April 12, illegal alien Eri Otoniel Roblero-Perez was allegedly driving under the influence and killed two boys on their bicycles in Spartanburg County, South Carolina. The two victims, 12-year-old Dereon Robinson and 9-year-old Mikhail-Lee Smith, were riding their bikes on the sidewalk when Perez jumped the curb, ran them over, ultimately killed them. Roblero-Perez was charged with two counts of felony DUI, open container, and driving without a license. He was also placed under a detainer from ICE.
(Fox Carolina, April 2026; WSPA 7, April 2026; WTOC 11, April 2026; NBC 4, April 2026)
Josue Abraham Chirino-Leonice (April 12, 2026)
On April 12, Venezuelan national Jose Abraham Chirino-Leonice allegedly murdered his co-worker, Juan Antonio Salinas Leija, with a sledgehammer in Harris County, Texas. However, he was released into the country by the Biden administration.
(DHS, April 2026; Fox 26, April 2026)
Luis Antonio Angel Orduno (April 15, 2026)
On April 15, Mexican national Luis Antonio Angel Orduno was driving under the influence of alcohol when he lost control of his car, slammed into a nearby building, and killed his passenger, 31-year-old Luis Mayoral Moguel, in Carroll County, Kentucky. After receiving treatment for his injuries, Orduno was detained and charged with Vehicular Homicide, DUI 1st Degree, No Operator’s License, No Insurance, and Criminal Mischief 1st Degree. He has an immigration detainer hold, and it is unknown when and where he entered the country illegally.
(Kentucky State Police, April 2026; Madison Courier, April 2026)
Said Jama Ahmed (April 14, 2026)
On April 14, DHS arrested Somalian national Said Jama Ahmed for alleged ties to Somali piracy and falsely forging and using a passport. Ahmed was taken into CBP custody after being reported by an off-duty Canadian police officer for walking towards the U.S.-Canada border. However, this is not Ahmed’s first contact with U.S. officials. In March 2012, he and nine other armed pirates were encountered and fingerprinted by the U.S. Navy after taking an Indian ship hostage. Ahmed then entered the United States illegally in September 2022 and was detained by ICE officials in 2024. He was extradited in April 2025.
(DHS, April 2026; Fox 11, April 2026)
Roman Ceron Amatitla (April 14, 2026)
On April 14, ICE lodged a detainer against Mexican national Roman Ceron Amatitla, who is accused of randomly setting a building on fire on March 16 that killed four people in New York City, New York. According to the Queens District Attorney, Amatitla entered and exited the building several times before the incident, then went to a nearby gas station where he bought a beer and grabbed a pack of matches. He returned to the building, lit a piece of paper on fire, and placed it in the stairwell trash can. Afterward, as the building went up into flames, Amatitla drank his beer as he watched the building go up into flames and residents struggled to evacuate. Among his victims is a 3-year-old child. (AOL, April 2026; Fox News, April 2026)
Dipakkumar Ghelani (April 16, 2026)
On April 16, Indian national Dipakkumar Ghelani was arrested by the Florida Highway Patrol for allegedly trafficking cannabis with a street value of over $13 million in Jacksonville, Florida. Once in custody, ICE took custody of Ghelani thanks to the Florida Highway Patrol’s 287(g) law enforcement partnership with ICE. During his interview with immigration officers, he was unable to provide documentation proving his legal presence.

The two suspects were taken into custody following the search and charged with trafficking cocaine, and Ruiz-Juarez was charged with carrying a concealed weapon. (Gaston County Government, April 2026; WBTV 3, April 2026)

Loudoun County Sheriff’s Office, April 2026; Fox 5, April 2026)
Roni Mendez-Escobar (April 22, 2026)
On April 23, Guatemalan national Roni Mendez-Escobar was arrested after a court appearance in Fairfax County, Virginia, by ICE Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) for possession of child pornography. Mendez-Escobar was initially arrested for this crime in October 2025, with ICE issuing a detainer against him on October 23. However, on October 27, Fairfax County politicians released him from custody without notifying ICE. Once in DHS custody, it was announced that Mendez-Escobar had been deported three times in 2015, before reentering the country again at an unknown place and time.
(DHS, April 2026; ABC 7, April 2026)
March 2026
Orvin Bayardo Fuentes-Borjas (March 3, 2026)
On March 3, the Irving Police Department responded to a tip and arrested Honduran national Orvin Bayardo Fuentes Borjas after searching his phone and finding 50 images of child sexual abuse materials. He was charged the same day. On April 1, ICE lodged a detainer against Fuentes-Borjas and shared that he was issued a final order of removal on February 3, 2020.
(DHS, April 2026; Irving Journal, March 2026)
Samuel Antonio Maldonado-Erazo (March 4, 2026)
On March 4, Honduran national Samuel Antonio Maldonado-Erazo allegedly beat his three-year-old nephew to death in Cantonment, Florida. Following the mother’s deportation in January 2026, Maldonado-Erazo was the child’s primary caretaker. Maldonado-Erazo brought the child to work with him and ignored the child’s signs of distress throughout the day. Eventually, first responders were called, finding the victim in cardiac arrest and taking him to the hospital. Unfortunately, the three-year-old died. According to the Escambia County Sheriff, the child had extensive bruising across his body, several burn marks, several broken ribs – one of which was detached from the backbone – a broken collarbone, and a transected pancreas, which raised concerns of possible sexual abuse. Maldonado-Erazo was then taken into custody and charged with negligent manslaughter, but his charges may be upgraded. According to ICE, he entered the country illegally with his daughter in August 2021, but they were later released due to the Biden administration’s catch-and-release policies. 
(ICE, March 2026; Fox 10, March 2026; ABC 3, March 2026; TFP, March 2026)
Conrrado Ahuexoteco Atrisco (Incident Feb. 25, arrested March 5, 2026)
On March 5, Mexican national Conrrado Ahuexoteco Atrisco was arrested for allegedly sexually assaulting a 14-year-old high school student in Park City, Utah. The incident was reported to the Park City High School resource officer on February 25. According to the victim, she was at her friend’s house, lying in her bed and playing on her phone, when the friend’s ex-boyfriend, Atrisco, asked if he could join her. Atrisco then got onto the bed and tried cuddling with her, then pulled down her pants and sexually assaulted her. Following the report, the Park City Police Department obtained a search warrant for Atrisco’s DNA and began attempting to locate him. Once located, Atrisco allegedly gave the police a false name and denied all wrongdoing. He was later taken into custody, and the arresting officer requested that Atrisco be held without bail. The same day, ICE lodged a detainer against him. ICE reported that Atrisco previously entered the country illegally, but he was removed by Border Patrol. He then illegally reentered a second time, but this time the Biden administration marked his immigration case as a non-enforcement priority and released him into the country. 
(DHS, March 2026; ABC 4, March 2026; VOZ, March 2026)
Franquin Inestroza-Martinez & Gerzon Jose Chirinos-Munguia (Incident Jan. 7, arrested March 5, 2026)
On March 5, Sunnyvale Department of Public Safety detectives arrested Honduran nationals Franquin Inestroza-Martinez and Gerzon Jose Chirinos-Munguia for the alleged shooting and murder of 24-year-old Kembery Chirinos-Flores. ICE previously lodged a detainer against Chirinos-Munguia in 2019, but it was not honored, and he was released back into the community. 
(DHS, March 2026, City of Sunnyvale, March 2026)
Sukhdev Singh (March 6, 2026)
On March 6, Indian national Sukhdev Singh allegedly struck a 65-year-old pedestrian, who remains in critical condition, with his semi-truck in Indianapolis, Indiana. When police responded to the scene, they arrested him after discovering that Singh had a non-domiciled CDL which was issued in January 2026 by New York. Later that day, Sukhdev Singh was released and immediately taken into ICE custody, where he remains. It is still unclear when or where he entered the country illegally. 
(DHS, March 2026; Times of India, March 2026; Financial Express, March 2026)
Bairon Posada-Hernandez (March 8, 2026)
On March 8, Honduran national Bairon Posada-Hernandez was arrested after allegedly shoving two men onto the New York City subway tracks. His victims, 31-year-old John Rodriguez and 83-year-old Richard Williams, survived at the scene; however, a few days later, Williams, an Air Force veteran, passed away from his injuries. On March 10, Posada-Hernandez was arrested for attempted murder and had an ICE detainer lodged against him. Prior to this, he had racked up fifteen charges, including domestic violence and aggravated assault. In a press release, ICE revealed that Posada-Hernandez has been deported four different times – most recently in 2020 – and it is unknown when or where he reentered for the fifth time. On March 25, he was indicted on charges of second-degree murder. 
(DHS, March 2026; PIX 11, March 2026; The Hill, March 2026; New York Post, March 2026)
Erasto Lopez-Gomez (March 11, 2026)
On March 11, Mexican national Erasto Lopez-Gomez allegedly killed a 62-year-old man in a fatal hit-and-run in Pitt County, North Carolina. The victim, Christopher Babcock, was riding his motorcycle towards Greenville, North Carolina, when Lopez-Gomez turned left in front of him and caused a collision. Lopez-Gomez then fled the scene, and Babcock later succumbed to his injuries. Babcock leaves behind a wife, two stepchildren, and a sister. After being located and taken into custody, USCIS confirmed that Lopez-Gomez is an illegal alien who entered the country at an unknown time and place. He remains in custody.
(WFIN, March 2026; Fox News, March 2026)
Patel Visa Fraud (March 13, 2026)
On March 13, the U.S. Attorney’s Office announced that eleven Indian nationals in Kentucky, Massachusetts, and Ohio were arrested and charged with conspiracy to commit visa fraud. The suspects allegedly set up staged armed robberies, so the store clerks would be able to apply for a U visa. USCIS may grant U visas to “victims of certain crimes who have suffered mental or physical abuse and are helpful to law enforcement or government officials in the investigation or prosecution of criminal activity.” These allow the holder to get a work permit, and, under certain conditions, visa holders may be eligible for permanent residence after a few years. The eleven suspects, all surnamed “Patel”, are accused of allegedly arranging a robbery or paying for themselves or a family member to be a “victim.”

One of the suspects, Rambhai Patel, was previously charged and convicted in New York in December 2023 for conspiracy to commit visa fraud. According to court documents, Rambhai and his co-conspirators set up and carried out staged armed robberies at convenience stores and fast-food restaurants across a few states. All of this was done in front of security cameras, so when the victims called the police, they could offer their help and qualify for a U-visa. The U-Visa Program has been rife with fraud since its inception in 2000, and police agencies have been bombarded with fraudulent applications or reports of fake crimes.
(Breitbart, March 2026; USAO, March 2026; USAO, December 2023; USCIS)
Samir Ousman Alsheikh (March 16, 2026)
On March 16, a federal jury in Los Angeles, California, convicted Syrian national Samir Ousman Alsheikh, who was the former head of Syria’s largest civil prison, Adra Prison, under the rule of President Bashar al-Assad. Alsheikh was convicted of torture and lying to U.S. immigration officials about his background to fraudulently obtain a green card and attempting to naturalize as a U.S. citizen. According to evidence from his victims, from 2005 to 2008, Alsheikh inflicted severe mental and physical pain and suffering on prisoners. A form of torture that he was accused of carrying out on prisoners was known as the “magic carpet.” An inmate would be strapped to two wooden panels with hinges in the middle. The guards would then bend the inmate in half, and sometimes stomp on the device, which resulted in serious injury, including broken spines. After his tenure at Adra Prison, Alsheikh briefly served as Governor of Deir Es-Zour, a critical oil-rich region on the Syria-Iraq border, and where he was also accused of brutal crackdowns on dissidents.

It is believed that Alsheikh entered the United States and settled in Los Angeles, California at some point in 2020. Shortly after, he applied for U.S. citizenship. In 2022, the Syrian Emergency Task Force alerted the United States that Alsheikh was in the country, and in July 2024, a complaint was filed that Alsheikh lied on his visa and citizenship applications about having never persecuted any person on any basis and having never been involved in killing or trying to kill someone. He was then taken into custody. After a two-week federal jury trial, he was convicted and is now awaiting sentencing.

Illegal Infiltration & Fake Documentation:-A Real Case I Handled

Home Minister @AmitShah ji has held that the population of Muslims in India has increased due to illegal infiltration. Let me share a real case I personally handled about 5–6 years ago in Mumbai, one among many that reveal how deep this problem runs. Please do read to understand the rot.

1. The Client’s Request:- One evening after court hours, a Muslim gentleman known to me came to my office. He had given his premises in Govandi, Mumbai, on a leave and license agreement to a family of 6/7 people.
Even after the agreement expired, the family refused to vacate.

I perused his papers and assured him of appropriate legal action. He then asked if the matter could be resolved sooner than usual.
When I explained that such cases typically take little time, he hesitated and what he said next stunned me.

2. The Shocking Revelation :- He quietly said, “Sir, those tenants are not Indians, they are Bangladeshis.”

That single sentence changed everything. Two thoughts struck me instantly:
1. Why hadn’t he mentioned this earlier?
2. How did they even get valid Aadhaar and PAN cards as visible in the agreement?

3. The Investigation:- On examining the documents, everything looked perfectly legitimate; Aadhaar, PAN, ration card, even voter ID.
We filed RTIs, involved the local police, and began to dig deeper.

Gradually, the truth surfaced, the birth certificate forming the basis of all these documents was forged.

Using that single forged certificate from 1967, the accused had created a full legal identity for himself and his family, including Aadhaar, PAN, ration card, and voter ID.

4. A Web of Fraud:- It didn’t stop there. The man had used the same method to obtain documents for his wife and children. His son was even married to an Indian Muslim woman, effectively merging into the Indian population.

During the investigation, we uncovered an organized network, a full-fledged industry operating to regularize illegal immigrants by manufacturing fake Indian identities that pass every verification test.

5. The Larger Problem:-India’s diversity makes such infiltration even easier. People entering from Bangladesh, Pakistan, Myanmar, or Nepal often resemble locals making visual identification almost impossible.

Add to this the corruption that exists from border checkpoints to administrative offices, and you have a perfect ecosystem for illegal population growth.

In this very case, we found the involvement of certain officials, and shockingly, even a few lawyers.

6. A Moment That Exposed the Rot:- One of those lawyers, representing the Bangladeshi accused, told my Muslim junior,
“How can you do this? This is a matter of religion.”
My junior stood firm and warned him of a complaint before the Bar Council.

This single moment revealed how some individuals, blinded by religious or political motives, are actively protecting those who illegally enter and settle in India.

7. The Unanswered Question:- 
This wasn’t the only case, I have come across several similar ones.
Despite being aware of this menace for years, successive governments have failed to implement a robust national mechanism to identify and deport such individuals.

8. The Hope:- Now that the Home Minister himself has spoken openly about the issue, one can only hope it translates into real, concrete action. India needs a firm, technology-backed, corruption-proof mechanism to detect and remove non-Indians living here on forged documents.

Illegal infiltration is not just a demographic concern, it’s a threat to national integrity, law, and fairness. The time for acknowledgment is over.
The time for action has arrived.

April 3, 2024. Police show up at a teacher's house in Illinois with a search warrant. Her 3 kids are inside.
They tell Alley Bardfield she's under arrest for having sex with an 11-year-old student she invited over for a "play date."
She looks at them and asks: "Me?"

In the video below, bodycam shows the whole arrest, from the knock on the door to the patrol car.

She was a long-term substitute for a 6th grade class in Decatur, in her 30s, the "fun teacher" on TikTok. According to court documents, she wrote her phone number on the classroom wall for her 11-year-old students.

For months she messaged one of the boys. She sent him $700 on Cash App, bought him headphones worth more than $400 and sent him inappropriate photos on Snapchat. On March 29, 2024, she had him over to her house.

His mom noticed he was acting differently, checked his phone, and he told her everything. The next day they went to police. Hours before the arrest, with police and his parents listening, Bardfield called the boy and told him to delete their messages.

At the door she denied everything. In the patrol car she kept denying it, until the detective said he had seen the photos. Then she said: "He kept asking and asking and wouldn't leave me alone."

Then she added: "I have my criminal justice degree. I'm in my master's program. This isn't how I want my life to be."

She was fired, and in August 2025 she pleaded guilty to predatory criminal sexual assault of a child. She faced up to 60 years. Prosecutors asked for 40. The judge gave her 10, and she'll be on the sex offender registry for life.

The boy's family is now suing the school district. Their lawyer says they believe there may be more victims.

text:
Delhi Police asks X to take down IFF's account and posts. IFF will challenge the notices in court unless they are withdrawn.

The Delhi Police has asked X to remove the Internet Freedom Foundation's account, six of its posts, the accounts of SFLC and @geoblockedindia, and posts by 16 other users, on the ground that they defame the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. The posts document and comment on a legal notice sent in the RSS's name to IFF, SFLC and @geoblockedindia, which demanded that the three stop criticising and documenting government blocking orders. IFF received copies of the two police notices from X on the morning of 3 November 2026.
IFF calls on the Delhi Police to withdraw both notices. If they are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court.

What has happened

On 29 October 2026 at 9:54 PM, IFF, SFLC and the operator of @geoblockedindia received a two-page "legal notice" said to be issued on behalf of the RSS. It asked the three to stop opposing the government's blocking directions, stop documenting restricted content, stop posting details of geo-blocked posts, and confirm in writing within seven days that they would comply. It was signed by an unnamed "Authorised Signatory". Several RSS office-bearers have since said on X that the notice is not authentic. IFF replied to the notice, wrote to the RSS at its official address asking whether it had authorised it, and published both the notice and its reply on 30 October.

On 31 October 2026 at 8:06 PM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police, filed an "Illegal Content Report" with X (reference LD-321926). It listed two posts: IFF's post of 30 October on the notice, and SFLC post of the same day. The stated reason was that the posts are "defamatory towards the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023". The boxes for "safety/security", "defamation" and "other" were ticked. The fields for the nature of the court order and court order details were left empty. The desired action was "Remove/withhold content".

On 1 November 2026, a second notice arrived in the RSS's name. It said the matter had been handed to the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, that complaints had been filed in several states, and that requests had been made to block IFF's X account and suspend the organisations. The Delhi Police had made its first request to X the previous evening. IFF did not know this until X told it on 3 November.

On 2 November 2026 at 8:51 AM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) filed a second notice with X (reference LD-322956). It lists 40 URLs. Thirty-seven are posts. Three are the entire accounts of @internetfreedom, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. This time the boxes for "Hate speech", "defamation", "safety/security", "enforcement of court order" and "other" were all ticked. The court order fields were again left empty. The stated reason reads: "The posts constitute defamation and illegal content under Section 356 BNS. Under Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, read with Section 79(3)(b) IT Act, lawful notices require action within 3 hours."

The 16 other users are @ProdctiveUseful, @PanjwaniManoj, @jidge_, @RatanSharda55, @baxiabhishek, @SchrdingersDbag, @ashleshbiradar, @seemay, @NasirHussainINC, @Being_creat_ive, @AjoyDharmavaram, @othlaw, @_ananyaaa, @AimPoojaind, @incorigibleBhai and @rraoind. Their posts, as far as IFF can tell, comment on the notice or on the notice about it.

X forwarded both notice to IFF on 3 November 2026, at 8:47 AM and 10:03 AM, saying it was doing so "in the interest of transparency" and that IFF may wish to seek legal counsel and challenge the request in court. X's emails do not say that it has acted on the requests. The Delhi Police has not written to IFF, and no court has been approached, as far as the reports disclose. SFLC and @geoblockedindia have separately reported notifications from X about requests from the Uttar Pradesh Police, the Telangana Police and the Delhi Police's Cyber Crime unit, one of them against the whole of the @geoblockedindia account.

IFF's position

IFF condemns this legal action. A police force has made itself the enforcement arm of a private legal notice whose authenticity the organisation it names has not confirmed, and whose demand was that three organisations stop documenting censorship. The notices would deliver exactly what the notice asked for as they would also remove the accounts of the three groups in India that keep public records of what is blocked, and of who ordered it.

The posts in question are about a legal notice sent to us. They quote it, criticise how it was drafted, and say that we will carry on with our work. A person who receives a threat is entitled to publish it and answer it and that is not defamation of the sender. 

In the three weeks before the first notice, IFF assisted 86 people whose accounts were suspended or whose posts were withheld in India. SFLC's Free Speech Tracker recorded about 268 content restrictions and 83 account restrictions in the first 29 days of October. @geoblockedindia publishes the orders behind such blocks when platforms disclose them. None of this is unlawful. Documenting censorship and challenging it in court is what the Constitution expects of citizens.
IFF will not delete the posts. If the Delhi Police does not withdraw the notices, we will challenge them in court.

Why the reports are unlawful

Defamation is not a police matter. Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is a non-cognizable and bailable offence. Under Section 222 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, no court can take cognizance of it except on a complaint by the person aggrieved. 

Under Section 174 of the BNSS, the police cannot investigate a non-cognizable offence without an order of a Magistrate. The Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) is not the person aggrieved. The notices disclose no complaint by the RSS and no order of any Magistrate. Whether a statement is defamatory is for a court to decide after hearing its author, with the defences of truth, fair comment and good faith available to that author. 

In Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India, (2016) 7 SCC 221, the Supreme Court upheld criminal defamation on the strength of these safeguards. A police officer who asks a platform to remove speech as defamatory has decided the question himself, without a complainant, a court or a hearing.

The posts are protected comment. Exceptions 1 to 3 to Section 356(1) protect the truth published for the public good, opinion on the public conduct of public servants, and opinion on the conduct of any person touching a public question. The posts publish a notice that was sent to us and give our opinion of it. The RSS, if it sent the notice, chose to enter a public question. If it did not, the posts defame no one.

Further, Section 79(3)(b) and Rule 3(1)(d) do not permit this. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down Section 79(3)(b) so that an intermediary acquires "actual knowledge" only through a court order, or a notification from the appropriate government or its agency that unlawful acts relatable to Article 19(2) are being committed. The court said that it would be difficult for intermediaries to judge the legitimacy of the millions of requests they receive, and that the burden must not be placed on them. Rule 3(1)(d), as amended in November 2025 and February 2026, now requires the intimation to come from an officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary or Deputy Inspector General, to be reasoned, and to specify the legal basis and the nature of the unlawful act, subject to a monthly review by a Secretary-level officer. The three-hour window the notice invokes applies to a lawful order that meets these conditions. A web form that ticks "hate speech" and "enforcement of court order" while leaving the court order fields blank, and that gives one sentence of reasons for 40 URLs, is not such an order.

The notices by the Delhi Police are disproportionate. They seek to remove three accounts in their entirety, with years of posts, over six, four and eleven posts respectively. They sweep in 16 third parties whose only connection is that they commented on a public controversy. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that any restriction on speech must be necessary, proportionate and the least restrictive measure available, and that orders restricting speech must be published and reasoned. Removing an organisation's entire account for criticising a legal notice fails each of these tests.

The effect is to silence documentation of censorship and providing legal aid to Indian internet users. The accounts named are those that record blocking orders in India. The notice asked them to stop. A takedown request that accomplishes the demand of an anonymous private notice is not law enforcement. It is the use of state power for a private end, which Article 14 forbids.

Our demands

1. To the Delhi Police: Withdraw reports LD-321926 and LD-322956 and confirm the withdrawal in writing to X and to IFF. 

2. To the Delhi Police: Disclose the complaint on which the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) acted, the authority under which the reports were filed, and whether any order of a Magistrate under Section 174 BNSS exists. Disclose every request made to any platform in this matter, including those made by the Cyber Crime unit against @geoblockedindia.

3. To X: Do not act on the reports. If any content is withheld in India, tell the affected user before acting, give them the full request, and name the legal basis. Publish both reports to the Lumen database, as the reporting form itself contemplates.

4. To the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and the Ministry of Home Affairs: Have the Secretary-level review required by Rule 3(1)(d) examine these intimations, and tell police forces that Rule 3(1)(d) is not a remedy for defamation, which the law reserves to the person aggrieved and to the courts.

5. To the RSS: State publicly whether it authorised either notice or any complaint to the police. If it did not, say so to the Delhi Police.

If the notices are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court. We will continue to document blocking orders, to publish them, and to provide legal assistance to anyone whose account or post is withheld in India. Nothing in these notices changes that.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

text:
Last night IFF, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia received a legal notice said to be issued purportedly on behalf of the RSS. It’s hard to believe this comes from an organisation that has had a century to practise its paperwork and hence this may even be a weird prank! This notice asks us to stop criticising the Government’s blocking orders and stop documenting them. It also wants us to confirm in writing within seven days (seriously).

We can tell it’s an excellent teaching aid and here are seven lessons from it.

1) Say who you are: The notice names no advocate and gives no enrollment number. It is signed by an “Authorised Signatory” with no name. Replies go to a free Proton Mail ID, and the “office” is a residential flat in outer Delhi. A notice that can’t tell you who sent it is less a legal document than a weather event.

2) Have a grievance of your own: It never says how its client is harmed when we criticise a MeitY advisory. It complains on behalf of the Government’s blocking orders. The Union has no shortage of lawyers, and it hasn’t asked for volunteers.

3) Name the law: It threatens “appropriate legal action” under “the applicable provisions of law” and doesn’t cite a single section of any statute. A threat with no law, is literally an empty threat.

4) Don’t ask people to give up a fundamental right within seven days: The first demand is that we stop “publicly opposing” government directions. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court held that discussion and advocacy of a cause, however unpopular, sit at the heart of Article 19(1)(a). Opposing an order is how its legality gets tested. That is the Constitution working as intended.

5) Check whether the courts asked for the thing you want stopped” In Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Supreme Court held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be made available so people can challenge them. The Reddit order is on the public Lumen Database because Reddit put it there. Reading a public database and saying what’s in it has a name. It’s called research.

6) Show us the spark and the powder keg: The notice says our work weakens national security measures, but it gives no instance, date or harm. In S. Rangarajan (1989), the Supreme Court held that the danger feared from speech can’t be remote, conjectural or far-fetched. It has to be like a spark in a powder keg. A post about a Lumen filing is not a spark.

7) Read it once more before you press send: The paragraphs run 1, then an empty 2 and 3, then 4. A PIN code wanders into the facts. The account it targets is on “Twitter”. 

Our reply is short. The notice is legally deficient because it makes no material allegation and cites no illegality. We will respectfully continue to advance constitutional rights, as we have done before. Notices like this rarely expect to win in court. They expect the recipient to get tired. We often are tired, but it has never changed what we do. Solidarity with @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. 

If your post or account has been blocked in India, write to legal@internetfreedom.in.
